title: From Systems of Record to Systems of Context — Omri Bruchim & Tomer Ast, monday.com

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk focuses on precomputing context layers and building durable user profiles versus live signals to construct the working set the model sees.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The talk focuses on precomputing context layers and building durable user profiles versus live signals to construct the working set the model sees.

summary: Omri Bruchim and Tomer Ast, engineering managers at monday.com, present the company's transition from a system of record to a system of context. They observe that when users ask AI assistants 'what should I focus on right now?', they get disconnected bullets—even though the assistant has access to all boards, tasks, emails, and Slack messages. The problem is not data retrieval but understanding. Systems of record capture what happened but not what it means. monday.com is a work platform where work lives—projects, tasks, decisions, meeting notes, and action items are all logged. Their AI personal assistant, Sidekick (also called Psyche), is designed to understand the user, their business, and work patterns while keeping the user in control. They identify three reasons context is hard: the agent gap (agents excel at known tasks but guess at priorities), records without meaning (logs lack context for why things happened), and the impossibility of building understanding at runtime. Their solution is the Monday world model—a precomputed context layer, not a bigger prompt or longer context window. It is built from two engines: a slow engine that mines weeks of activity to create a durable profile of who the user is and how they work, and a fast engine that reads recent activity to understand what is urgent and who the user is collaborating with. This split mirrors complementary learning systems in neuroscience (hippocampus and neocortex) and lambda architecture in data processing. Context is precomputed offline; when the user engages with Sidekick, a thin layer of logic is recomputed for recent activity and the full context is served to the agent. The system degrades gracefully when sources fail, understands urgency for proactive notifications, and compounds over time as profiles sharpen. The talk concludes by showing how Psyche answers the original focus question: the slow engine builds a profile (role, projects, location, work hours, daily patterns) while the fast engine surfaces immediate action items (commitments to others, unread VP emails, things said in Slack but not in standup). The speakers summarize that the bottleneck was never data capability but understanding how to connect the dots—and even the most capable agents (Claude, Gemini) cannot understand you without preprocessing. Honest limits include the model trailing live data, new users lacking data, and signal bias making it hard to separate signal from noise.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The core problem with AI assistants is missing understanding, not missing data or retrieval capability
Systems of record store what happened but not what it means—connections and meaning must be built separately
Context must be precomputed ahead of time, not constructed at runtime when a user asks a question
The Monday world model uses a slow engine (durable user profile from weeks of data) and a fast engine (live signals from recent activity)
The slow/fast engine split mirrors complementary learning systems in neuroscience and lambda architecture in data processing
Even the most capable agents—Claude, Gemini—cannot understand you without preprocessing context beforehand
The system compounds: more data sharpens profiles, adding sources is cheap and only contributes
Sidekick can judge urgency and decide when to proactively notify versus stay silent
Limitations include model lag behind live data, cold-start for new users, and signal bias creating noise
Distinguish between retrieval and understanding as distinct AI challenges

sections.title: From system of record to system of context
sections.summary: Omri and Tomer introduce the talk's thesis: decades of software recorded what happened but never understood connections between records. They want to move beyond storing events to understanding relationships.

sections.title: The gym answer: data without understanding
sections.summary: Omri shares that when he asked Claude what to focus on, it suggested going to the gym. Despite having access to all boards, tasks, emails, and Slack messages, the assistant produced disconnected bullets. The problem is never missing data or retrieval—it is missing understanding.

sections.title: monday.com, Sidekick, and where work lives
sections.summary: The speakers introduce themselves as engineering managers at monday.com, a work platform used by hundreds of thousands of teams. monday.com is where work lives—not just records. They describe Sidekick (also called Psyche), an AI personal assistant that understands the user, their business, and their work patterns while keeping them in control.

sections.title: Three reasons context is hard
sections.summary: Three challenges: the agent gap (agents excel at known tasks but guess at priorities), records without meaning (a log never says what it means, illustrated with a git blame analogy tracing code to a customer complaint), and the impossibility of building understanding at runtime—context must be precomputed ahead of time.

sections.title: The Monday world model
sections.summary: They introduce the Monday world model: a context layer that understands who you are, how to help you, and what not to do. It is not a bigger prompt or longer context window. The problem is understanding how entities connect, not retrieving data.

sections.title: The data model and its two engines
sections.summary: Tomer explains the data model built from thousands of data points: work structure (entities and relationships), current snapshot (live signals like urgency and collaborators), and durable profile (patterns and cadences over time). Two engines run on different time windows: a slow engine mines weeks of activity into a durable profile, and a fast engine reads recent activity for live signals. One knows you, the other knows your day.

sections.title: Why the split mirrors the brain and lambda architecture
sections.summary: The slow/fast split mirrors complementary learning systems in neuroscience (hippocampus captures experiences instantly, neocortex distills durable lessons) and lambda architecture in data processing (speed layer over recent window, batch layer over full history, merged into a served view).

sections.title: How it comes together, and the honest limits
sections.summary: Data is collected from Monday, Slack, email, and calendar, then precomputed offline into data structures, signals, and patterns. At serve time, a thin slice of logic is recomputed for recent activity and the full context is served to Sidekick. The system degrades gracefully (sources isolated, falls back to last verified context), understands urgency for proactive notifications, and compounds over time. Limitations: model trails live data, new users lack data, and signals carry biases.

sections.title: Answering the question with Sidekick
sections.summary: Omri shows how Psyche answers 'what should I focus on right now?' The slow engine builds a durable profile—role (engineering manager), projects (Psyche and Notaker), location (Tel Aviv), daily hours, and work patterns. The fast engine surfaces immediate action items from the past day or few days: three commitments promised to others, an unreply to a VP's email, and something said in Slack but not in the daily standup. The speakers summarize that the bottleneck was never data capability but understanding how to connect the dots. Even the most capable agents—Claude, Gemini—cannot understand you without preprocessing context beforehand. This is what Psyche and the Monday world model aim to solve. They invite questions and direct attendees to find them near the stage and on LinkedIn.
